idiom_name: Promise.all / Promise.allSettled for the latch; Atomics.wait/notify over SharedArrayBuffer in workers
implementation_notes: In the single-threaded event loop the one-shot latch is a language idiom: Promise.all(tasks) (or Promise.allSettled when every outcome matters) needs no counter and blocks no thread, but Promise.all completes successfully only when every input fulfills (and rejects on the first rejection), while allSettled waits for every input to settle; an input that never settles still leaves the fan-in pending, so apply a timeout or cancellation policy. A genuine multi-thread rendezvous exists only inside worker_threads: a SharedArrayBuffer viewed as Int32Array, Atomics.add to arrive, Atomics.wait to sleep on a generation value and Atomics.notify from the last arriver. Blocking is forbidden on the main thread (Atomics.wait throws a TypeError when the current thread cannot be blocked), so page code uses the promise form or Atomics.waitAsync when it must observe a shared phase without blocking.
pitfalls: Atomics.wait cannot block the main thread (TypeError) and SharedArrayBuffer is gated by cross-origin isolation in browsers, so the same barrier code works inside a worker and fails in the page.
Promise.all rejects on the first failure while the other promises keep running to completion: without cancellation (AbortSignal, worker termination) the survivors leak work.
A hand-written 'wait until the counter reaches N' loop that yields with setTimeout or awaits a tick still occupies the loop and can livelock when the counter is only advanced from a microtask.
Atomics.wait returns 'not-equal' when the value changed before the call and 'timed-out' on expiry - treating it like a guaranteed block misses both races and timeouts.
